title: Robust Quantum Key Distribution Arbitrarily Close to Local Correlations
abstract: Recently, Wooltorton et al. [Phys. Rev. Lett. 132, 210802 (2024)] and Farkas [Phys. Rev. Lett. 132, 210803 (2024)] have exhibited the mismatch between Bell inequality violations and their cryptographic application in device-independent quantum key distribution, by showing that arbitrarily close to the set of local behaviours there exist quantum correlations guaranteeing a constant rate of secret key. While these results require correlations attaining the maximum quantum value of a suitable Bell observable (aka the Tsirelson bound) and rely on a kind of ideal self-testing of a maximally entangled state and associated Bell measurement, here we show that the effect is robust: for every one of the Bell inequalities considered by Wooltorton \emph{et al.}, a constant rate of secret key ensues if the observed Bell violation is sufficiently close to the respective Tsirelson bound. For these and also the Bell inequalities of Farkas, we furthermore present numerical results based on semidefinite relaxations of the minimum min-entropy consistent with a certain Bell violation, which demonstrate that small but nonzero key rates can be guaranteed (in principle) by practical and efficient means.
summary: This paper establishes the robustness of device-independent quantum key distribution by showing that a constant secret key rate can be guaranteed even if the measured Bell violation is only slightly below the theoretical quantum limit. Using semidefinite programming and a robust self-test framework, the authors provide theoretical and numerical evidence for practical key generation rates. This advances the field by quantifying the tolerance for imperfections in real-world quantum devices.
main_problem: To demonstrate that the security of device-independent quantum key distribution (DIQKD) remains robust and guarantees a constant key rate even when the observed Bell violation is only slightly less than the theoretical maximum (Tsirelson bound).
main_result: The authors prove that a constant, non-zero secret key rate can be guaranteed if the observed Bell violation is sufficiently close to the respective Tsirelson bound for the considered Bell inequalities.
method: The work employs a 'robust self-test' approach, utilizing semidefinite relaxations of the minimum min-entropy consistent with a given Bell violation to derive lower bounds on the key rate.
model_or_system: The analysis focuses on DIQKD protocols involving two parties (Alice and Bob) using uncharacterized devices, whose security is tested by measuring violations of specific Bell inequalities.
key_observables: Bell Inequality Violation ($\eta$), Key Rate ($R$), Tsirelson Bound ($	au$), Classical Bound ($ eta$).
important_parameters: The deviation parameter ($\epsilon$) quantifying how close the observed violation is to the Tsirelson bound.
main_assumptions: The analysis is based on specific families of Bell inequalities and assumes the asymptotic (i.i.d.) limit for the key rate calculation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the key rate as a function of the Bell score, showing the rate remains non-zero even as the violation approaches the classical boundary.
paper_structure: The paper builds upon previous work by extending the key rate guarantee from requiring the absolute maximum Bell violation to requiring only a sufficiently close approximation to that maximum.
why_interesting: This work provides theoretical guarantees on the practical feasibility of QKD, showing that small experimental deviations from ideal quantum correlations do not necessarily lead to a complete loss of cryptographic security.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Lower bound on the conditional entropy H(A|E, X = 0) versus observed Bell score η ∈(β(θ, ϕ, ω), τ(θ, ϕ, ω)) for the Bell correlator Tθ,ϕ,ω [15]. The chosen parameters (θ, ϕ, ω) move the quantum correlations arbitrarily close to the local boundary while main- taining a CHSH violation ≳2 and c0, c1 > 0. The numerical SDP relaxations complement the analytical results by detailing key rates under sub-maximal violations (η < τ): while positive key distillation remains theoretically robust near maximal violations (η →τ), the curves steepen sharply as local limits are approached, showing that allowable experimental noise shrinks rapidly.

Figure 2: Plot of H(A|E, X = 0) versus η for β = 0.2, 0.15, 0.1, and 0.05 for the Bell inequality used in [16]. While the theoretical maximum key rate remains robust near ideal violations (Bd →1), smaller values of β cause the curve to steepen sharply, demonstrating that noise tolerance shrinks rapidly as quantum correlations approach the classical bound- ary.
